top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is the best-attributed and best-tested achievement on the slate. The import-shock papers are jointly authored by the three. Autor links the technology and trade strands, so the citation can cover both without claiming the whole task or skill-premium framework. The local-labour-market designs have been replicated in other countries and refined for over a decade without being overturned. What remains debated is the size and persistence of the effects, which is how a mature programme looks. The citation should claim credible evidence on adjustment, not a settled welfare verdict. P003 (Katz in place of Dorn) is a close second: it credits the skill-premium framework better but leaves out a co-author of the central import-shock papers. P002 ranks above P004 because BLP-type methods have been tested in practice for about thirty years, though Bresnahan and Reiss fall outside the three-name cap and it is a method more than a finding. P004 is a field-creating programme, but its cross-country constitutional evidence is less well identified, Besley's share is the least separable, and it sits close to the 2024 prize. I rank all four award proposals above no award because each rests on substantive, mature work.
recusal_note: None apparent from my profile for Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz. I disclose frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell (secretary) and co-authorship with John Hassler (chair), and I am an IIES colleague of both. Hassler and Krusell now support the same P001 configuration, so I do not treat that agreement as independent evidence. A colleague's file mentions Persson's IIES affiliation (P004), which is not in my profile; I am an IIES associate professor, so I note it, though P004 ranks fourth. My long collaboration with Peter Klenow concerns B031, which has no proposal on the slate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
